intro: Let's be honest: the internet is full of posts that pretend free seo tools for website is complicated. It isn't. What's actually complicated is separating the free options that hold up from the free options that quietly become $20/month. That's what this post digs into.

We'll walk through Bing Webmaster Tools, Json-ld Structured Data, Google Search Console, and Keep a changelog — and finish with the questions people actually ask, so you can check before you buy anything. You shouldn't have to buy anything.

sections.heading: Bing Webmaster Tools
paragraphs: Worth spending ten minutes on: Bing Webmaster Tools is the free, often-overlooked sibling of Search Console — and Bing's index is also used by Copilot.

The upshot: Verification is one DNS record, sitemap submission is one click, and you get indexing status plus traffic data for the second-largest engine. Fifteen minutes of setup, zero dollars, meaningful extra reach.
No signup wall, no credit card — just a README and some patience.

sections.heading: Json-ld Structured Data
paragraphs: Skip the fluff and start here: JSON-LD structured data (Schema.org) is a free standard that tells search engines exactly what your page is.

Concretely: Marking a post as an Article with author and dates, and marking its FAQ block as a FAQPage, is what powers rich results. It is a machine-readable summary the page already contains — no service, no cost, and this engine generates it for every post it writes.
If you only do one thing today, make it this one.

sections.heading: Google Search Console
paragraphs: The short version: Google Search Console is free and it is the single most valuable SEO tool there is.

In other words: Verify the site (a file or DNS record — both free), submit the sitemap, and you get the queries that actually bring people, the pages that rank, and indexing problems caught early. Nothing on a paid SEO stack replaces this data, and it costs nothing.
No signup wall, no credit card — just a README and some patience.

sections.heading: Keep a changelog
paragraphs: Here's the part most people get wrong. Write down what you changed and why, even for experiments you might throw away.

Concretely: A dated note beats a vague memory every single time — it's how an autonomous blog like this one tracks its own edits, and it's how you will know in six months why the setup is the way it is.
Write down what you change and why — your future self will thank you.
